title: TA8-23946
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of the People's Republic of China (PRC), claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS
The claimant alleged as follows:

After being convinced by her boyfriend, XXXXX of the benefits of prayer for his mother's health, which was proven by her improved recovery from a stomach tumor, the claimant began to embrace the concepts of Christianity. In XXXXX of 2006, she joined an unregistered church and attended twice-monthly on a regular basis until a Public Security Bureau (PSB) raid in XXXXX of 2007, which sent her boyfriend into hiding as well as herself. With the assistance of a smuggler, the claimant was able to safely exit China on a false Taiwanese passport. Once in Canada, she learned of her boyfriend's capture and detention in China and was able to provide proof of his detention
The claimant fears that, if she returns to China, she will be arrested and jailed for her religious activities.
The Panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity

The Panel determines that the claimant's supporting documentation, which includes her Resident Identity Card (RIC)2 and household register (Hukou)3 establishes her identity as a citizen of the People's Republic of China (PRC). Credibility

The determinative issues in this claim are the credibility of the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF)4 narrative, her initial immigration interview and oral testimony with regard to her religious activities in China and Canada and her pursuit by Chinese authorities.

Credibility is an issue in all claims before the Immigration and Refugee Board. In order to determine whether the claim is well founded, the Panel must find, on a balance of probabilities, that the evidence is credible and trustworthy. A claimant's testimony is presumed to be true unless there are valid reasons to doubt its truthfulness.5 The existence of contradictions, discrepancies, and implausibilities in the evidence of a claimant is a well accepted basis for a finding of a lack of credibility. This also applies to omissions in the claimant's previous statements, whether made to Canadian immigration officials at the time of arrival in Canada, in previous examinations under oath or at the hearing of the claim, or in the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF). Attendance at an Unregistered Church in China

A determinative issue with regard to this claim is whether it is credible that the claimant actually attended or participated in the associated activities of an unregistered church in China from XXXXX of 2006 until XXXXX of 2007. The Panel finds the material aspects of this testimony contained little detail with regard to the Sunday service that took place on a twice-monthly basis and the precautions employed by this unregistered church to avoid discovery by the Chinese authorities.

The claimant was asked to describe a typical service in detail. The Panel noted that the claimant was hesitant when describing a typical Sunday service at her unregistered church and that she simply described a few mechanical parts of the service. In the opinion of the Panel, the claimant's description can only be described as sparse in that the person-in-charge led them in a recital of the Lord's prayer, he would read a specific scripture from the Bible, they would discuss this passage, they would all pray together and, finally, the leader announced arrangements for the location and lookouts for the next meeting. When prompted as to whether she wished to expand upon her description, the claimant added that the leader actually blessed them before they left. When the Panel asked her about the precautions employed at her unregistered church, which the Panel noted included that the members exit the premises in small groups, the claimant indicated that the two look-outs were the main precautions employed and that there was an escape plan. When prompted to describe the escape plan, the claimant simply indicated that they were to "flee fast" and she added that remote locations were used to avoid discovery of their services by the Chinese authorities. When prompted as to what the escape plan actually entailed, the claimant simply indicated that they must leave by either the front or back door or whichever exit the PSB were not approaching, and, if surrounded by the authorities, it was best to leave by the back door since there was a road located at the back of the home, which led to a mountain. Although given another opportunity to expand upon her response, she could not remember any other safety precautions. When prompted about each attending members' respective Bible, the claimant added they had been instructed to take the Bibles with them and she did confirm that this was considered to be a safety precaution.

In assessing the claimant's description of a typical religious service in China, notwithstanding that she only attended these services approximately twice a month for approximately five months or a total of ten occasions in China, in the opinion of the Panel, the claimant simply named a few mechanical parts of a typical Sunday service and she did not describe any other interactions among the members or between the person-in-charge and the attendees at a typical Sunday service in any significant detail. Similarly, the Panel notes the claimant only gave a brief description of the safety precautions employed at her unregistered church to avoid discovery by the authorities. As well, the Panel had to prompt the claimant about the prior arrangements that had been discussed by the members as to what was to be done with the Bibles if the authorities came and it notes that her description of the escape plan only referred to leaving quickly and, if possible, escaping to a road at the rear of the location. In the context of the claimant's brief description of the Sunday services at her unregistered church, her limited knowledge of the precautions employed to avoid discovery and the simplistic outline of the alleged escape plan, the Panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant did not attend an unregistered church in China. Credibility of the Claimant's Corroborating Document

A determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's corroborating documents with regard to her testimony and PIF narrative. The Panel finds that specific identity features of the Prison Visitor's Card did not correspond to the documentary evidence with regard to gender of the holder of the Prison Visitor's Card and the lack of dates on the card.

The claimant's initial PIF6 indicated that her boyfriend had been arrested while trying to escape from China and, during her oral testimony, she confirmed that he had been caught while trying to enter Russia and was presently in detention. In support of her evidence of she presented a photocopy of a Prison Visiting Card7, which she alleged had been carried to Canada from China by a friend of the claimant's mother to support and give credibility to her refugee claim. The claimant confirmed that the picture on this document was that of her boyfriend's mother, XXXXX XXXXX; however, the Panel noted that the corresponding Resident Identity Card (RIC) number, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX [emphasis is mine], on this Prison Visiting Card could not belong to this individual since, according to the documentary evidence8, the second last number on the RIC denoted that this person was a male. The Panel noted the other identifying information was correct, such as the name, the date of birth of XXXXX XXXXX and relationship to the prisoner (his mother) and then gave the claimant an opportunity to explain the discrepancy of the gender on this specific document. The claimant was unable to explain the discrepancy of the wrong gender number denoted on this RIC as outlined on the Prison Visitor's Card.

The Panel also noted, with regard to other Prison Visitor's Cards, which have been presented as evidence in previous hearings that the Panel has presided over at the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB), that these documents usually have dates stamped or filled in by hand that indicate when the cardholder visited the prisoner, who was identified on the document. The claimant was asked a series of questions that pertained to this document. The Panel noted that the claimant was hesitant in her responses that she did not know the present location of where the individual was who had given her this document or whether he was in still in Canada, the document's appearance was like this when given to her and she indicated that the document had been given to her two weeks or three weeks prior to this sitting date. The Panel also notes that the manufacture and distribution of forged documents9 of all descriptions are common in China. In the context that the Prison Visitor's Card contains an obvious deficiency with regard to the cardholder's gender as identified in the documentary evidence10, as noted by the Panel, that specific information with regard to visitation dates was absent from this document when compared to similar documents that have been presented at other IRB hearings that the Panel has presided over and that the documentary evidence11 indicates that fraudulent documents are easily obtainable in the PRC, the Panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has embellished her testimony by submitting a fraudulent document to support her evidence. The Panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's submission of a fraudulent document. Pursuit by Agents of the Chinese Government

A determinative issue in this claim is whether it is credible that the PSB are pursuing the claimant for her religious activities. The Panel finds that the claimant's testimony evidence with regard to this issue is neither reasonable nor credible.

The claimant learned that Mr. XXXXX, her church leader, and one of his friends had been arrested by the PSB on XXXXX, 2007, but her boyfriend was able to escape. After the claimant went into hiding, she alleged that the PSB came to her home a week after the PSB raid search of her whereabouts as well as going to her boyfriend's home in search of him. In fact, the claimant testified that the PSB have gone to her home on more than twenty occasions and the last occasion was as recently as XXXXX of 2009. The claimant's amended PIF12 indicated that the PSB are still searching for the claimant. Notwithstanding the number of occasions the PSB have been to her home, to the claimant's knowledge, no summons or arrest warrant has ever been left with her family. The documentary evidence13 indicates that it is very common in China for a summons to be left with family members, especially when the person named on the summons is not easily locatable. The latter documentary evidence does indicate that procedures for issuing summonses are not consistently followed by all PSB offices across China; however, the Panel notes that the claimant is from XXXXX City, which is an urban centre of approximately 1.3 million people. In the Panel's opinion, the PSB of a large urban centre would be well versed on proper issuing procedures for summonses, it would have a large police force because of the sheer size of its population and it is reasonable that there would be continuity of any documents issued by the PSB, which would include summonses. The Panel determines, if the PSB were so intent on locating and arresting the claimant, that it does not seem reasonable or plausible that they would not leave a summons with her family considering the number of times, manpower and resources that they are alleged to have expended in searching for her whereabouts. When this latter determination is considered as well as the finding above that the claimant has embellished her evidence by submitting a fraudulent document in the form of a Prison Visitor's Card, the Panel further determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not being sought by the Chinese authorities for her alleged religious activities. Use of an Illegal Passport to Exit China
The Panel finds that material aspects of the claimant's testimony with regard to her departure from China were neither reasonable nor credible nor plausible.

The claimant alleges she was able to use the services of a smuggler to assist her in her departure from China and this individual was able to obtain a fraudulent passport for her. The claimant indicated in Schedule 1 - Background Information at her initial immigration interview14, that allegedly the passport that was provided for her was Taiwanese and it was green in colour but she admitted that she was never shown the passport and that it was never in her possession. Specifically, the Panel notes that the claimant admitted that she was never told by the smuggler, who assisted her in her exit from Hong Kong to Canada, the actual name she was to travel under. The claimant's counsel submitted a number of cases, including the case of Song15, which the Panel has reviewed and within that decision was the case of Zhang16 that stands for the proposition that the smuggler would have only had to bribe one official to assist in her successful departure from China.

To be fair to the claimant and in an abundance of caution with regard to counsel's submissions, the Panel has reviewed Zhang17 with regard to the issue of the ease of the claimant's departure from China.

The Panel determines that the name that the claimant was to travel under was critical to the claimant's successful exit from China in 2007 and may have been requested by any number of airport or government officials in either China or Canada. The Panel notes that the claimant in Zhang18 left China in 2005 but this case is not on point since the claimant in that proceeding testified that she used her own passport to leave China and not a fraudulent passport as is the case in this proceeding. As well, the Panel believes the passage of time has brought about increased security measures at all airports in China. Specifically, the documentary evidence19 outlined above notes the increase of security measures at airports in anticipation of the Beijing Olympic Games as well as the fact that "immigration officials in China are carrying out "stronger" document verifications."20 The documentary evidence21 indicates that all persons who seek to leave China, foreigners as well as Chinese citizens, are required to present their travel documents to security officials. In the context of the claimant's lack of knowledge associated with her passport information and the documentary evidence, as outlined above, the Panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's testimony with regard to her departure from China is neither credible nor plausible. The Panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's testimony with regard to the ease of her departure from China. Is the claimant a genuine Christian today?

The Panel notes that the claimant's documentary evidence22 includes a supporting letter from the Pastor of the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, which indicates that the claimant has been regularly attending services there since XXXXX of 2007, and was baptized23 on XXXXX XXXXX, 2008. The Panel has no evidence to rebut the fact that the claimant attends this church in Toronto and has been baptized. In the opinion of the Panel, neither of these documents attests to the claimant's motivation to attend her present church. As well, the Panel believes that the mere possession of a pastor's letter or a baptismal certificate is not in itself a definitive basis for finding that the claimant is a genuine practicing Christian. For these reasons, the Panel gives the correspondence from the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and the Baptismal Certificate little evidentiary weight.

The claimant appears to have a basic grasp of the concepts of Christianity and was able to answer a number of religious and Biblical questions that were put to her over the course of this sitting. The Panel is also aware that, during her responses to the immigration officer's questions at her initial immigration interview24, the claimant did not appear to be very knowledgeable about what role Jesus Christ played in Christianity. The claimant was given the opportunity to explain her responses with regard to the immigration officer's questions about the relationship between Jesus Christ and Christianity. The claimant did remember this question and admitted that she did not answer it well. The claimant explained that she did not know what part of Christianity she should talk about. The claimant's counsel has submitted that since the Panel does not know the exact questions that have been asked, the CIC notes and the immigration officer's assessment should not be taken into consideration by the Panel.
The Panel does not agree.

The claimant has been given the opportunity to explain her answers at CIC Interview and she has admitted that she did not respond to these questions well. No other responses arising out of this interview have been challenged as to whether the information that was recorded by the immigration officer is reliable or not, therefore, the Panel determines that the CIC notes and the immigration officer's assessment of the claimant's Christian knowledge will be considered by the Panel.

The claimant's present knowledge of Christianity is quite reasonable when the Panel considers that she was first introduced to the concepts of Christianity in XXXXX of 2006 by her boyfriend through prayers for his mother. In addition, according to her PIF narrative, her boyfriend also taught her some knowledge of Christianity, she had been attending twice-monthly services in China since XXXXX of 2006 to XXXXX of 2007, she had been present at the unregistered services on at least one occasion when a pastor was present and she had observed Holy Communion on this date in XXXXX of 2006. As well, the claimant has been attending religious services at the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX since XXXXX of 2007, which is approximately thirty months as of the date of this sitting, and she has attended Baptismal classes in Toronto. However, in observing the claimant, the Panel noted that at no time during the hearing did the claimant appear to have an emotional commitment to the Christian faith.

The Panel has made previous determinations above that the claimant did not attend an unregistered church in China, that the claimant has embellished her testimony and submitted fraudulent documentation in the form of a Prison Visitor's Card to support her claim, that she is not being pursued by agents of the PSB and that the ease with which she exited from China to Canada was neither reasonable, credible or plausible. In the context of these latter findings and in considering the assessment of the immigration officer that the "Subject was not very knowledgeable about Jesus Christ;" the Panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that whatever knowledge of Christianity the claimant possesses, it was acquired in the thirty months since she first arrived in Toronto and only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim. For these reasons, the Panel determines that the claimant is not a genuine practicing Christian.

On the basis of the cumulative findings and negative inferences noted above, the Panel determines that the claimant has not satisfied her burden of establishing a serious possibility that she would be persecuted or that she would be personally subjected to a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a risk of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China. Conclusion

The Panel concludes that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, rejects her claim. (signed) "Paul G.C.
